title: A hard chapter
hook: the ancients, it says, kept people simple rather than clever, a line scholars read in very different ways (Tao Te Ching 65)

segments.voice: Yesterday, beneath your feet: the long journey starts where you already stand. Your line was beneath my feet. What did you start from right where you were? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

Some lines in old books make a reader put the book down. Chapter sixty-five of the Tao Te Ching has one. On a first reading, it sounds like advice for keeping people in the dark, written for rulers who'd like their subjects easy to manage. Some readers stop there, and that's a fair place to stop. Others go back and read it again. Today, a hard chapter, and what happens when you read it twice.
screen: `A LINE THAT STOPS A READER.` → `KEEPING PEOPLE IN THE DARK?` → `WHAT IF YOU READ IT TWICE?`

segments.voice: First, what it says. In James Legge's translation, the ancients who were skilled in the Tao used it "not to enlighten the people, but rather to make them simple and ignorant." The chapter goes on: people are hard to govern when they know too much. Ruling a state by cleverness, it says, is a thief to the state. Ruling without it is a blessing. Second, the first reading. Taken at face value, that's a ruler's dream: keep the population uninformed and it stays easy to manage. Some readers take the chapter exactly that way, and are troubled by it. That reaction deserves room. The text says what it says. Third, the second reading. The Chinese word behind simple is the same word chapter twenty uses when the speaker of the Tao Te Ching calls their own heart the heart of a fool, while everyone else seems bright and sure. Read with that in mind, some hear plain and unscheming rather than kept ignorant, and the target here may be scheming cleverness, the kind that games every system. And notice who the chapter warns most sharply: the ruler who governs by cleverness. Fourth, why read it twice at all. The chapter doesn't settle which reading is right, and neither will today. But a hard line read once tends to become a verdict. Read twice, it becomes a question. That habit is useful well beyond old books: the email that stung, the headline, the comment from a parent. The second reading doesn't always change the meaning. It changes how fast you decide.
screen: `NOT CLEVER, BUT SIMPLE.` · `A FIRST READING TROUBLES.` · `A SECOND READING: UNSCHEMING.` · then, large: `READ IT TWICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a hard passage twice. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Here's the line again, the gist of it: the ancients did not make the people clever, but simple. Hear it once the way it first lands, as control. Notice what rises: suspicion, maybe, or a shrug. Let that be. Now hear it again, with simple meaning plain, unscheming, like the speaker's own fool's heart in chapter twenty. Notice what shifts, and what doesn't. You don't have to pick a winner. Just hold both readings side by side, the way you'd hold two cups, one in each hand. The bell holds the time.
A hard chapter. Chapter sixty-five's line about keeping people simple, read in more than one way. Today's word.
Your line: read it twice. When something rubs you the wrong way today, a message, a headline, a page, read it a second time before you answer. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching differ over chapter sixty-five: some read it as advice to keep people uninformed, others as praise of plainness over scheming, and some readers go through it slowly, more than once, to weigh both.
